title: Cluster 03 DRILL: Diseases, Antibiotics, Vaccination and Epidemiology
subtitle: H2 Biology 9477 · Book 9, Extension Topic A · 10 questions · 87 marks · 32 parts · one mark per minute, so a little under an hour and a half · every question is an actual exam paper question except five parts labelled CONSTRUCTED
los_html:
Learning outcomes, against the questions that test them.
(a) innate and adaptive immunity, the four types of immunityClusters 1 and 2; assumed here
(b) roles of B and T lymphocytes, APCs and memory cellsQ2(b), Q3(c), Q3(e), Q6, Q8(a) as reach-back
(c) antibody structure related to function, IgGQ4(b), Q4(c), fused with (i) by the specimen itself
(d) somatic recombination, hyper-mutation and class switchingCluster 2
(e) vaccination stimulating immunity without causing the diseaseQ6, Q8(b)
(e) vaccination of a high enough proportion breaking the transmission cycle, herd immunityQ6, Q7(a), Q7(b), Q7(c), Q9(e)
(e) the eradication of smallpox as the named caseQ6, Q9(e)
(f) benefits and risks of vaccinationQ7(c), Q8(a), Q8(b)
(g) influenza virus and the epithelial cells of the respiratory tractQ1(a), Q1(b), Q1(c)
(g) HIV and helper T cellsQ2(a), Q2(b), Q2(c), Q3(e), Q5(b)
(h) modes of transmission of bacterial pathogensQ3(a)
(h) modes of infection, virulence factors and evasion, using M. tuberculosisQ3(b), Q3(c), Q3(d), Q3(e)
(i) modes of action of antibiotics, including penicillinQ4(a), Q4(b), Q4(c), Q5(a), Q5(b), Q5(c)
(j) R0 as an indicator of transmissibility, and predicting outbreak progressQ9(a) real, Q9(b), Q9(c), Q9(d), Q9(e) constructed
(k) outbreak, epidemic and pandemicQ10(a) real, Q10(b), Q10(c) constructed
reach-back Book 1: quaternary structure, denaturation and loss of epitope conformationQ4(c), Q8(b)
reach-back Book 4: antigenic drift, the RNA genome and the resistance boundaryQ1(b), Q5(c)
reach-back Cluster 1: phagocytosis, phagosome and lysosome fusion, inflammation, interferonQ1(a), Q3(b), Q3(c), Q3(d)
reach-back Cluster 2: helper T lymphocytes, memory cells, the secondary response, the antigen-binding siteQ2(a), Q2(b), Q3(e), Q4(c), Q6

One primary concept each, checked for duplicated required answers and not only duplicated labels. Q1 how a virus destroys the tissue it infects · Q2 how a virus disables the immune system itself, and virulence read off two graphs · Q3 one bacterial infection from droplet to ruptured tubercle · Q4 penicillin, and the specimen's own antibody-against-antibiotic comparison · Q5 the boundary of what antibiotics cannot act on · Q6 the named eradication case at essay scale · Q7 herd immunity read off real vaccination data · Q8 the benefits and risks weighed, with a documented reject list · Q9 R0 defined, applied and computed · Q10 the spread ladder, defined and applied.

Where two questions touch the same clinical fact they need different paragraphs. TB in an AIDS patient appears three times and each time from a different outcome: Q2(a) explains the helper T cell loss under (g), Q3(e) explains the ruptured tubercle under (h), and Q5(b) explains why an antibiotic is prescribed at all under (i). Herd immunity appears in Q6 as part of the smallpox case, in Q7 as a data interpretation, and in Q9(e) as an arithmetic consequence of R0; none of the three schemes credits the same sentence.

No viral replication cycle is set anywhere in this drill. Reproductive cycles of enveloped viruses and retroviruses are Core Idea 2 LO 2(e), antigenic shift and drift are 2(f), bacterial genetics and antibiotic resistance are 2(g), and all four belong to Book 4. Q1(b) reaches into 2(f) deliberately as the Book 9 to Book 4 bridge, and Q5(c) marks the resistance boundary so you do not revise it here.
